title: Mowgli
author: Rudyard Kipling
short_summary: A man-cub called Mowgli is taken in by a wolf pack in the Indian jungle and grows up under the Law of the Jungle. Baloo the bear teaches him, Bagheera the panther buys his life with a freshly killed bull, and Kaa the python pulls him out of the worst trouble he ever gets into. But Shere Khan the tiger has claimed Mowgli since the night he arrived — and sooner or later the man-cub will have to settle it.
extended_summary:
Mowgli comes to the wolves as a baby, crawling into their cave the night Shere Khan the lame tiger is hunting him. Father Wolf and Mother Wolf keep him, and at Council Rock the Pack has to decide whether he may stay. Baloo the bear, who teaches the wolf cubs the Law of the Jungle, speaks for him; Bagheera the black panther buys his life with a freshly killed bull; and the Pack lets him in.

Mowgli learns the Law and the Master Words — "We be of one blood, ye and I" — which let him claim help from every people of the jungle. The one people who have no Law are the Bandar-log, the monkeys, and when they carry him off to the ruined city they call the Cold Lairs, it takes Baloo, Bagheera and Kaa the rock python to get him out. Kaa, whom the monkeys fear more than anything, is the one who ends it.

As Akela, the old leader of the Pack, weakens, Shere Khan gathers the young wolves against Mowgli, and Mowgli fetches the Red Flower — fire — from the village and drives the tiger off with it. Later he goes to live among people, is taken in by a woman called Messua and set to herd buffalo; and when Shere Khan comes for him at last, Mowgli splits the herd, drives it in from both ends of a ravine and kills the tiger there. Then the villagers decide he is a sorcerer and stone him out, and Mowgli goes back to the jungle, belonging fully to neither side.

questions.prompt: At Council Rock the Pack must decide whether to let the man-cub stay. How is his life bought?

options: Bagheera pays for him with a freshly killed bull
Baloo promises to teach the whole Pack for a year
Father Wolf offers his own place in the Pack
Akela hunts alone for a season in exchange

questions.explanation: Baloo speaks for him and Bagheera pays. The price is remembered against Mowgli for years — when the young wolves turn on him, they are reminded that he was bought into the Pack with a bull, and that the debt has never been cancelled.

questions.prompt: Baloo teaches Mowgli the Master Words of the jungle, so that any people will help him: "We be of one ___, ye and I."
questions.explanation: Mowgli learns them for the hunting people, the birds and the snake people, and they save him more than once. It is the most useful thing Baloo ever beats into him — and Mowgli complains bitterly about the lessons at the time.

questions.prompt: The Bandar-log — the monkey people — are despised by everyone else in the jungle. Why?

options: They have no Law, no leader and no memory
They kill far more than they can ever eat
They cannot climb as well as they boast
They live in the ruins that people built

questions.explanation: They boast, forget, start things and never finish them, and the rest of the jungle refuses to speak of them at all. Kipling makes them the one people with no Law in a book where the Law is everything — which is exactly why they are dangerous.

questions.prompt: The monkeys carry Mowgli off to the Cold Lairs. Who finally frightens them into giving him up?

options: Kaa the rock python
Chil the kite
Hathi the elephant
Akela the lone wolf

questions.explanation: Baloo and Bagheera cannot manage it — a hundred monkeys are more than a bear and a panther can handle. It is Kaa, whose name the Bandar-log cannot bear to hear, who empties the ruins; and Baloo and Bagheera have to look away from his dance themselves.

questions.prompt: Put the events of Mowgli's life in the jungle in the order they happen.

items: A baby crawls into the wolves' cave with a tiger behind him
Bagheera pays a bull for the man-cub's place in the Pack
Baloo teaches him the Master Words of the jungle
The monkeys carry him off to the Cold Lairs
Mowgli brings the Red Flower up from the village
Shere Khan is killed in a ravine by a buffalo herd

questions.explanation: Every step is a debt or a lesson coming due. Mowgli is bought, taught, rescued and finally does the paying himself — the tiger who claimed him on the first night is killed by a boy who has learned to use both the jungle and the village.

questions.prompt: Match each character to what they are to Mowgli.

right: The bear who teaches the cubs the Law
The black panther who paid for his life
The lone wolf who leads the Pack
The jackal who runs at the tiger's heels

questions.explanation: Kipling sorts his jungle by what each animal is worth: the teacher, the protector, the leader and the flatterer. Tabaqui, who has no strength of his own and survives by carrying tales for Shere Khan, is treated by the book with more contempt than the tiger.

questions.prompt: Mowgli belongs to two worlds and is never quite accepted by either. Sort each detail.

options.label: Learning the Law from a bear who cuffs him
Being reminded that a bull was paid for him
Running with the Pack at Council Rock
Being taken in by a woman called Messua
Being sent out every day to herd buffalo
Being driven away with stones as a sorcerer

questions.explanation: Each side takes him in and each side turns on him: the young wolves throw the bull in his face, the villagers throw stones. Mowgli ends the story belonging fully to neither, which is the real subject of the book.

questions.prompt: Mowgli goes down to the village to fetch the Red Flower. Why is fire the one thing that settles his quarrel with Shere Khan?

options: Every animal in the jungle is afraid of it, and he is not
It is the only weapon that can wound a full-grown tiger
The Law of the Jungle allows its use only against tigers
It proves to the Pack that he is a man and must leave

questions.explanation: Fire is the one thing in the jungle that belongs to people alone. The moment Mowgli can carry it, he stops being a weaker kind of wolf and becomes something none of them can face — and the same moment makes it certain that he will have to leave the Pack.

questions.prompt: Mowgli saves the village's cattle and kills the tiger that had been hunting the district for years — and the villagers drive him out with stones, calling him a sorcerer. Can you understand why they do it, or is it simply unfair? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both readings can earn full marks. A strong 'simply unfair' answer lists what Mowgli actually did for them. A strong 'you can see why' answer notices what the villagers see: a boy who runs with wolves, arrives with a tiger's skin and speaks to animals — and that Messua, who is kind to him, is put in danger by exactly that. Accept either, argued from the book.

questions.prompt: The Law of the Jungle has rules for everything — who may hunt what, when to call for help, how to behave at the water in a drought. Invent one more Law of the Jungle. What is the rule, and what problem between animals does it solve?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer states the rule in Kipling's flat, practical style and then explains what trouble it prevents — because that is how the Law works in the book: every rule exists because something went wrong once. A rule with no reason behind it is a weaker answer.

questions.prompt: The animals never call fire by its name. In the jungle it is known as the Red ___.
questions.explanation: They will not name it because they are afraid of it, and Mowgli notices that fear long before he understands what to do with it. Kipling gets an enormous amount out of the fact that animals have a different word for the one thing humans control.

questions.prompt: How does Mowgli finally kill Shere Khan?

options: He traps him in a ravine between two halves of a buffalo herd
He fights him at Council Rock with the Pack behind him
He drives him into the river where the crocodiles wait
He burns the dry grass around him with the Red Flower

questions.explanation: Mowgli splits the herd, sends one half in at each end of the ravine, and lets the buffalo do it. He does not beat the tiger by being stronger — he beats him by understanding cattle, ground and the fact that Shere Khan always sleeps after a heavy meal.
